inline.s: Only our Great Master — why does he appear in bodily form? For living beings’ sake he plays the host within the guest. His broad and long tongue-mark moves through space like wind; his thunder-voice, through the long night, wakes the sleeping multitude. He comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; to see our Master — thus, and just thus.
And two disciples followed after him

The Tathāgata sits in serene repose — why then does he walk in meditation? A thought flashed forth: to ferry living beings across. The venerable one follows after, chasing the wind and grasping at shadows. When all beings are ferried over, the fevered dream still has not woken.
Eulogy for the Sandalwood Vairocana Buddha (with preface)

The elder Sun Yunyi of Qu’a, courtesy name Tunan, was traveling as an official in the Southern Sea when he happened upon a branch of sandalwood, about a foot in girth and some eight feet long, such as the world counts rare. Delighted, he bought it, meaning to emulate the old story of Udyāna. Carrying it home, he presented it to the Guangfu Dharma-ground of his district, where the bhikṣu Tongtai shouldered the task, and so the wondrous form of Vairocana was completed. A hall was built to enshrine it, and a complete Tripiṭaka was further requested, together bringing the adornment to completion. At that time I was resting in old age at Nanyue, and Tongtai brought a letter begging a eulogy. Though I had never met the elder face to face, I rejoiced in his inconceivable merit, and so briefly set out the matter and praised it, saying:

Sandalwood from the seashore, its price beyond measure: a single grain of it is worth a thousandfold world. From where was it brought, to the land of China? No sooner is its fragrance heard than none fail to rejoice. Then there was an elder who met it without design, wishing to emulate Udyāna and fashion the marks of the wondrous form. With all his heart he exchanged for it, vowing it should become a Buddha; choosing a site he gave it away, and so gained Guangfu. There was then a bhikṣu endowed with great power of faith, who raised the burden in his heart; all was adorned with wondrous skill, and the thirty-two marks emerged from one man’s hand — as though from Tuṣita he displayed his awe-inspiring power. Perfected Vairocana, great gathering of merit, immeasurable radiance pervading every place, like a mote of dust split open: by good means, at one time there gushed forth the great thousandfold sūtra scrolls. The Buddha is originally without marks; they are formed according to the mind. The Dharma is originally without abiding; it takes form in response to conditions. By the elder’s mind, riding the bhikṣu’s vow, the Three Jewels of the world here appeared. The Dharma-realm is perfumed; those who touch it leave defilement behind. Whoever takes refuge at once empties all existences. The Dharma-body constantly abides; the land is rich and joyful. Scale and shell, feather and fur all receive liberation; blades of grass, motes of dust return alike to the Huayan treasury. Therefore our Tathāgata appears as the most honored among the honored.
Eulogy for Tejaprabhā, Tathāgata of Blazing Light

I bow to the Blazing-Light King of Radiance, whose universal shine fills the dust-motes of the ten directions. All the suns and moons over the four continents, all living beings receive his benefit. Sentient and insentient share one body, together entering the Tathāgata’s net of light. Body and mind, pores and motes of dust — all are perfectly transparent, nothing unpenetrated. The dreaming, inverted minds of living beings are altogether the Tathāgata’s treasury of light. Therefore the seven luminaries and the four hidden stars, the twenty-eight mansions each in its place, together make living beings’ bodies of marks; birth and death, coming and going, are all quiescence. The suffering of living beings is the Buddha’s mind; the Buddha is living beings’ sea of affliction. Since these two are without distinction, suffering and joy turn with the thought. Good indeed, son of the Buddha, that you accord with the Buddha’s mind and can hold the Tathāgata’s secret seal: thought upon thought forever pouring forth great radiance, able to shatter the darkness of beginningless affliction. All wondrous uses appear before him, flowing into the Tathāgata’s ocean of great vows, causing all who see, hear, and praise him to tread the ground of nirvāṇa’s eternal bliss.
Eulogy for Maitreya Rising from Sleep

All day he walks along the street, his two feet never resting; when tired he sleeps beneath a tree, his belly black as ink. Who has woken him? His dream-talk is not yet done. His whole body is weary, his bones ache; he stretches left and right and cannot shake it off. Such a village monk, too lazy to stir a sinew — how can you call him Maitreya?
Eulogy for the Pilgrim Maitreya

He bears his staff across his shoulder and slings a leather bag — a bundle of broken odds and ends — and trades it as rare merchandise. Meeting anyone he begs a single coin, not knowing they are all debts for a future life. He points to the estate beneath the Dragon-Flower Tree: reckoned up, the debt will still be owed.
Eulogy for the Bare-Bellied Maitreya
Why is his mouth open, laughing without cease? With belly bared and stomach bare — surely he fears the heat.
Eulogy for the Cloth-Bag Monk

Look closely: in his breast there is nothing; yet in his hand there is not nothing. Born into such shabbiness, he turns and laughs at others’ confusion. On his shoulder he bears his staff across; his feet are free and unconstrained. Were he not toyed with by little children, he could be called a bold and valiant man.
Eulogy for the Pratyekabuddha
Upon the great rock, beneath the tall pines, he sits upright, awakening to the unborn: the stream flows on, the flowers fall.
Eulogy for the Three Great Beings

These Three Great Beings appear in bodies according to kind: in heaven as gods, among humans as humans. Like the moon set in the sky, its shadow falls in many waters; the waters differ in clarity, the moon knows no this or that. Wisdom is their mother, hence their many children; compassion bestows joy, like the wish-fulfilling pearl. Their great vows are inexhaustible; the true sūtra is not letters. The mind of the Great Beings is just like empty space.
Eulogy for Mañjuśrī, the Great Being

The moon within the golden realm, the snow upon Mount Wutai; the lion-cub amid the clouds, the thunderbolt tongue in space. Who knows the old man who waters his ox? He is in truth the ambrosia of cessation. Sitting in serene repose in the Vajra Cave, he seems to crouch in a tiger’s den; a cup of tea in crystal glass, to cool the fever of affliction for a while. I ask you — how many people are in the cave? The three and three before and after are no idle tale.

Dwelling in the ground of quiescence, he raises the great Dharma-banner and beats the drum smeared with poison: all who hear submit their minds. Teacher of the seven Buddhas, father of living beings, like the lion king he strides with a broad and easy gait.
Eulogy for Samantabhadra, the Great Being

A half-rolled sūtra of the lotus, a single moon over Mount Emei; the world gleams like silver, his head white as snow. In ten thousand valleys the pine wind roars — all of it his broad and long tongue. Let the Dharma-realm be overturned as it will, empty flowers rise and cease of themselves. Buddha-lands enter the tip of a hair; the ten directions rest on his brow and lashes. The fragrant elephant charges on, pacing across the sky, trampling blind donkeys and lame turtles.

I bow to Samantabhadra, whose body is the Dharma-realm: motes, hairs, lands — sitting, lying, walking, standing. In the emptiness of Dharma-nature the great cloud spreads everywhere; because it is all-pervading, it knows neither going nor abiding. Hence his wondrous subtle marks are never hidden nor shown; whoever would see them must possess the universal eye. Riding the king of elephants, whose body is pure white — because originally undefiled, it is true purity. All saints and common folk do not depart from a single pore; the whole body, every part, surges like the ocean tide. The Great Being beholds me, and I behold the Great Being: emptiness meeting emptiness, originally without two. Therefore I bow in reverence to the great emptiness of the Dharma-realm; may we meet in every place, at every time.

His body measures with the Dharma-realm, the fountainhead of the ten thousand practices: what land or dust-mote does not fit within a single pore? The elephant king roams and wanders, unobstructed through the ten directions. I bow to him who is like space — vast, at ease, and free.
Eulogy for the Picture of Samantabhadra Bathing the Elephant

With the Dharma-realm as his body, where does he not go? Turning his back on this elephant king only brings toil and fluster. The elephant’s body is pure white, originally undefiled; washing it for no reason but adds specks of dust. Water does not wash water, white does not stain white: seek the two, and there is no distinction at all. Why then put the servant boy to such wasted labor? Where he does not reach, it becomes only more obstructed. As I see it, what is already complete is best: man and elephant both forgotten, saints and common folk swept away together.

The elephant’s body is spotless white — where could dust have stained it? A speck in the eye defiles the whole body. Wash it with water and the defilement only grows; leave it unwashed and it is clean of itself — no one knows why. Water adds nothing to purity, purity has no use for water; the two never meet. Such is the original state. The Great Being’s samādhi is the perfect fusion of the Dharma-realm: how could this dust-mote become a hindrance to him? To keep it is not defilement; to remove it is not purity. This phantom Dharma-gate is called non-contention.
Eulogy for Samantabhadra Riding the Elephant

With great practice and broad strides he treads the ten directions through: what pore, what dust-mote is there where he does not appear? Walking alone, sitting alone — how light and swift that is! To borrow another’s strength only brings confusion and disgrace. A lotus beneath his feet, the reins curled through the trunk — were it not for all this, he would be dragged down by it. Body and life lean on each other; coming and going, they have long grown familiar. Though it burdens him, it sets my feet at ease.
Eulogy for Samantabhadra, the Great Being, Empowering the Elephant

Our Great Being takes the Dharma-realm as his body: to any who uphold the sūtra he at once reveals his form. This is no display of supernatural power, no love of showing off; he would have living beings wake abruptly, here and now.
Eulogy for the Image of Great-Compassion Avalokiteśvara

I hear the Great Being is fundamentally without abiding, dwelling only in the thoughts of living beings. Since living beings are themselves the Great Being’s mind, why, being inverted, do they not see him? If one says the Great Being’s mind is inverted, how could he transform inverted people? And if living beings were not inverted, why should the Great Being labor to teach at all? Alas, people lack the light of wisdom: they lie drunk in broad daylight, dreaming all manner of dreams on fearful roads, terrified and panicked, unable to escape; they gallop and flee and cannot get away — like a thirsty deer racing after the heat-haze: the faster it runs the thirstier it grows, its strength and heart exhausted, and still it does not know it is inside a dream. The one who watches with waking eyes is moved to pity and shouts with all his might, yet the other does not feel the pain; and not only does he not feel it, he grows angry. Then he dreams again of pursuers, dreading those ahead and fearing those behind, and cries out with all his strength; at one cry he suddenly flings out his arms and starts up. From that one awakening he looks back at the dream and only then believes that his own mind gave rise to the inversion. Thus the Great Being can save from suffering; but he is much like the man with waking eyes. Though he may ever accord with living beings, the doubting grow only more frightened; yet if the person himself would but turn the light around for a moment, that would surpass the Great Being’s thousand hands and eyes. Good indeed, son of the Buddha — why be so inverted? If you do not seek within yourself but hunt for it in another, and if at the very place you hunt you see your own mind, then I too am named Avalokiteśvara.

The perfected one has no name; the name lies with people. He sees forms with the ear, hears sounds with the eye; the six functions are but one, and that one does not stand either. Pervading every realm and all space, there is no place he does not enter. The bright moon in the sky prints its light on a hundred rivers; like dew on grass-tips, every drop is round. At the tip of a single hair he manifests a wondrous body; sitting within a mote of dust he turns the great Dharma-wheel. In the blazing fire, on the mountain of knives, on the iron bed and the bronze pillar — one cry of utter distress, and suddenly it becomes a Pure Land. He chooses neither pure nor foul, makes no distinction of man or woman; if you would seek him, it is only within yourself.

I hear the Great Being divides his body into a trillion forms; eyes see and ears hear, yet none can tell which he is. When suffering comes they cry out, and crying out they are at once received; no coming or going is seen, no one knows who saves them. I now reflect: the Great Being is without self. At the gates of the six faculties he is like fire to whatever touches him: fire does not burn fire, dust does not stain dust. Because there is no this or that, he is named the Perceiver of the World’s Sounds.

The Great Being’s body is within the minds of living beings: intermingled yet not confused, apart yet not divided. Therefore when I have a request, he answers to the sound — not that the Great Being comes, but that I myself bear witness. If I did not know suffering, how could I make my plea? To know the very place of suffering: that is turning the stream back. Once my stream has turned, the Great Being is myself; seeking myself through myself — what could be amiss?

I contemplate the Great Being’s body: it is originally free of all marks. Because it is free of marks, it can manifest every kind of body — like the maṇi pearl, which shows all colors according to conditions. Thus Buddhas and bodhisattvas, the beings of the six paths, and even forms of other kinds: into all of them he enters. How then should one make distinctions of male or female body? If one sees the Great Being’s body as equal, without the mark of two, and understands that Dharma-nature is empty, then its radiance is like the full moon, and it can clear away the darkness of affliction, all at once, here and now. Therefore I take refuge in the Great Being and leap free of the suffering of birth and death.
Eulogy for Water-Moon Avalokiteśvara

His body like a drifting cloud, his mind like water and moon: unmoving yet responsive, wordless yet speaking. Call him and there is a sound; seek him and he is not found. Whatever suffering seeks him is wholly freed.

A water-moon bearing, an empty-flower surface, a valley-echo voice, a maṇi jewel. Wherever one meets him he shows his form; he comes and goes through the six paths with no dusk or dawn. His whole body and mind are only for others — where will you seek such a master?
A mirror image, water and moon, lightning in the vast void: touched, it stirs, and in a flash the shadow appears.
Not stained by a single mote of dust, openly displayed through the ten directions: a body covered with hands and eyes, needing no turning to and fro.
The mind is originally without affairs — for whom then these bitter thoughts? If someone comes asking, one does not know oneself.
The Great Being has no mind, yet answers like an echo to a sound: whoever has a request is answered as soon as he calls.
With a body without marks he answers the mind that seeks: nowhere does he fail to appear — he is named the Perceiver of the World’s Sounds.
The water flows into the sea, the moon never leaves the sky: responding without thought — this is the Chan of freedom.

The mark of no-mark: the mark is not in me. Appearing according to response, like fire meeting firewood — the thirty-two responses are still mere trifles; a billion and a trillion more — what should prevent them?
The Great Being’s body and mind are just living beings; therefore when vows are made, he comes as the response arises.
The perfected one has no form; true compassion makes no sound. Response and stirring meet in the Way: the sands are white, the water clear.
Taking wisdom as his life and beings as his mind, he seeks out the sound and saves from suffering: he is named the Perceiver of the World’s Sounds.

Body and mind transparent, like crystal; within and without made pure, like the moon upon a pool. He responds without being stirred, arrives without being sought; therefore my Master is called Inconceivable.

Speaking without sound, answering every request, like the echo answering the valley, like a precious mirror set before one — this is he who is named Avalokiteśvara; the samādhi he cultivates is called True Purity.

With a mind of quiescence he manifests wondrous marks: the full moon in the cold sky, its radiance measureless. I, with a refined mind, am like turbid water settling clear: the water clears, the moon appears, and no calculation is needed. The moon does not leave the water, the water does not leave the moon; since there is no coming or going, both are quiescent. My mind being still, the Great Being is myself; therefore what I seek is fulfilled as the thought arises.

Like an image in a mirror, like the moon in water: look, and it seems to be there; reach for it, and it cannot be grasped. With the sound of the ocean tide he puts forth his broad and long tongue — this is my Great Being’s rule of teaching the Dharma.

His Dharma-body is like a cloud filling the ten directions, born from emptiness like the light of water and moon. Because his body has no outside, his mind has no obstruction; hence in responding to things he attains great freedom. The thirty-two responses people call real are, for my Great Being, a single drop in the ocean. The afflictions of living beings are like a mad fire: let ambrosia be sprinkled, and at the thought they are cool.

I contemplate the Great Being as the moon in water, a branch of willow in hand, called the ambrosia of cessation: throughout the ten directions the world is moistened, and he can relieve living beings of the fever of the three poisons.

He responds without deliberation, pervades without thinking: spring comes and flowers open, the water clears and the moon appears. Hand grasps, foot runs; eye hears, ear sees. Far off, he is the more intimate; bland, yet never cloying. If a true man will but set his heart to bitter effort, the meeting will fulfill his life’s wish.

The Great Being’s body is originally without marks; it appears in response to the mind — a shape without shaping, a lightning flash, an empty flower, a mirror image, water and moon. Contemplate it thus, and suddenly one transcends.

In the ultimate void hangs the cool moon; its shadow sinks into many waters and admits no distinction. Thus the Great Being’s body is not two with things: wherever one sees or hears, there is no place it is not.

The Great Being is originally without body; his body appears according to living beings, as the moon reflects in many waters without distinguishing foul from pure. Dullness or brightness lies in clarity or turbidity, not in any choosing by the moon. Therefore, when the Great Being appears, one should contemplate with a pure mind; the contemplator’s mind being pure, all sufferings are emptied. If you would know the mind that saves from suffering, it is none other than the one who contemplates.

The Great Being does not think; his thinking is compassion. For living beings’ sake he sits dumbly, as if besotted. This besottedness and living beings cling together like glue and lacquer, and the two joined are past knowing. Thus he can save from suffering, shadow and echo at once. Therefore the Great Being’s compassion is deep and his vows heavy; but when the realm of living beings is emptied, his besottedness has no use.

I contemplate the Great Being as the moon in the sky: wherever there is water, it appears therein, choosing neither pure nor foul, for originally there is no this or that. Because the nature of water is empty, it has no dregs; the mind-water of living beings is likewise. Therefore whoever seeks has only to think, and he arrives. Because there are many waters, the moon shines everywhere; because there are living beings, the Great Being’s wonder is seen.
Eulogy for the Image of Avalokiteśvara Manifested as a Bhikṣu

Acting with purpose, responding without fixed direction — why forsake those others and manifest this one in true purity? Because the Buddha is no fixed thing, and without the Dharma who could transmit it? Were there no transmitter, the deaf and blind would all lie sleeping. Therefore the bhikṣu is the Dharma itself, the Buddha itself: his mind like space, like an echo issuing from the valley. Because space has no form, the blind can see; because the echo has no sound, the deaf can catch its meaning. Seeing and hearing do not abide; sound and form are both forgotten. By the power of samādhi he wakes the foolish and crazed: master within the dust, a lotus born in fire. Call his name and bow in reverence — he appears before you as the thought arises. Only then is my Master named as one who has attained the Chan of freedom.
Eulogy for Lotus-Leaf Avalokiteśvara

The sea of suffering has no shore — who will be the far bank? A single leaf of red lotus drifts along with the current. With this as boat he goes everywhere, missing no place. When creatures of every kind seek, he answers the stirring as the thought arises; therefore when his name is called, he appears through the universal gate.

The sea of suffering has no shore, the stream of desire never runs dry; what the perfected one relies on is a single leaf of green lotus. The far bank is not distant — no road is traveled. His body is like cloud and space, his mind like water and moon. Could one contemplate thus, what Dharma would there be to speak?
Eulogy for the Auspicious-Lotus Avalokiteśvara Carved by the Empress Dowager Cisheng

They say the udumbara flower appears but once in a thousand years; when a sage arises, it is taken as the sign. It is the Imperial Mother alone in whose palace this flower has grown: by this her virtue is attested — what more could be added?
Eulogy for Lotus Avalokiteśvara

The perfected one responds to things like the udumbara flower: few are they who see it, and so it is made much of. The green lotus rising from the water has its root in the mud; many see it, and so it is thought nothing remarkable. Therefore I say: the Dharma-body is all-pervading, praised throughout the ten directions, appearing through the universal gate. Thus complete and encompassing, why do people not know it? It is only before their eyes, raising the great Dharma-banner. Were it not true purity, this could not be brought about; and so the Great Being’s body is simply as it is.

The three realms have no safety — they are like a burning house; yet the perfected one dwells in them as in a land of coolness. The mire of the five desires is like a dung heap, yet the lotus rises tall, its stems and leaves growing of themselves. The maṇi pearl, pure and round in substance, fallen into a privy, loses nothing of its radiance. Buddha-nature in the midst of entanglement is soiled but not defiled: the lotus in the mud, the pearl in the latrine. In daily use, in action and rest, it is bright and undimmed. The lotus in the fire — therefore it is called auspicious.
Eulogy for Avalokiteśvara in Samādhi

With a mind of reflection he enters the thoughts of living beings: striking water he leaves a trace, knocking on space he makes a sound. Intermingled yet not confused, apart yet not two: an egret in the snow, a phantom in a pearl. Contemplating thus, he is named the most honored among the honored.
By the contemplation of illusion and the effortless power of wonder, through hearing, reflecting, and cultivating, he enters samādhi.

The Great Being has no mind — how could there be stillness or confusion? Living beings have no fixed nature — how could they be entangled at all? He ferries them in accord with conditions, yet originally has no such intention; suffering has no abiding place, like a sound in an empty valley. Therefore the Great Being’s compassion is the broadest: like space meeting space, like an echo answering an echo. Originally without coming or going, without arising or ceasing — the Great Being’s spiritual power is therefore beyond words.
Eulogy for White-Robed Avalokiteśvara
His robe is white, his heart is red; himself he has not, but only others. He causes all people to keep his name ever on their lips.
Originally undefiled, now likewise unstained: could one contemplate thus, the ten directions open clear.
A form without form appears with each stirring; in a single hair-tip its light is everywhere.
A broken bamboo branch serves as the auspicious grass; sitting, he cuts off the ten directions — the seas dry up, the mountains fall.
The seas run dry, the lotus withers; dust dissolves, awakening is verified — all by the willow branch that sprinkles and sweeps them clean.

I contemplate the Great Being’s mind: he would cleanse the defilement of living beings and so wears white himself, shielding their shortcomings. As water only washes away dust, and water does not wash water, so the Great Being and living beings in truth know no this or that. If you see your own mind, you know the Great Being’s face; split open a single mote of dust, and the Great Being’s radiance appears.

Within red, without white, the Great Being is in no way separated from the minds of living beings. Call, and the answer appears at once, like the bright moon held in turbid water. The mind’s stains of living beings are not easily removed, so the Great Being makes his own body their cleansing. If you would see the Great Being’s countenance in your daily life, seek it as form and it cannot be found: it lies only in one phrase, clear before the sound arises — heard by the eye, seen by the ear, past all speaking.

The Great Being is pure white because originally unstained; therefore he enters living beings, and his mind is not shallow. Like a water-clearing pearl cast into turbid water, the pearl keeps no shadow, yet the water clears to the bottom. The bright moon is in the sky: the water clears and it appears at once — uninvited it comes, unsummoned it pervades. Therefore the suffering of living beings is the Great Being’s body, and whatever is sought is the Great Being’s mind. Body and mind have no outside; this and that are not two. Appearing as the thought arises, he is named Inconceivable.

Deep and clear the cold sky, limpid the autumn water: the Great Being’s Dharma-body is truly like this. The moon does not leave the sky, the sky does not leave the water; they seem two, yet in truth there is no this or that. The mind is originally undefiled; the robe is not worn from love of white, but because those who are not white are made clean by gazing on him. The Great Being has no mind; living beings have thoughts, and the mark is born from the thought, like the moon in the palm. Therefore when there is a seeking, the response follows the thought: originally there is no coming or going — one’s own mind bears the witness.

The suffering of us living beings is itself the Great Being’s compassion; because suffering and compassion meet, my vows are never thwarted. Were there a hundred billion seeking, they would all be answered at once — how much less would he begrudge a wise man. Like quicksilver fallen to the ground, every drop is round: the one thing I seek, and every thing besides. I contemplate the Great Being’s body as one seeking an echo in an empty valley; the Great Being contemplates my mind as a thing seen in the palm of his hand.
Eulogy for Fish-Basket Avalokiteśvara
The basket is in her hand, her feet never stop walking; at the crossroads she would have people know that she is there.
One thing in her hand she can never put down; her true heart in every shred is spent for others without pretense. Therefore I say: she is one of true compassion.
Fish in hand, she hawks them in the street; her eyes search out people, seeking only to be quick. In her heart she cares not for half a coin — most likely she would settle compassion’s debt.
Eulogy for Purple-Bamboo Avalokiteśvara

The purple bamboo grove, the ground of seven treasures, the rock of Putuo, the vajra realm: sitting, he cuts off the ten directions, ever calmly at leisure. Whoever seeks him comes at the sound of his name. Were he not my Master Avalokiteśvara, who could grant every wish to each?
Purple bamboo is no grove; the Great Being is no body. What is seen now all comes forth from one’s own mind.
Eulogy for the Great Being Avalokiteśvara of the Southern Sea

Green sea and grey cliffs, yellow flowers and emerald bamboo, fish and turtles, dragons and yakṣas, dens of ghosts: he appears in form according to kind, emerging and sinking along the stream. Like space resting on the earth, there is no place where he is not complete. This is Avalokiteśvara’s body of freedom — not in vain is he called a Buddha of the past.

He sits upon the flat rock, contemplating the mind of quiescence; from all that stirs he brings forth a wondrous sound. The Dharma is free of marks; the true sūtra has no words. It is our Great Being who manifests bodies like clouds: every request is answered, no kind is left unvisited. With a mind of great compassion he is wholly one with deluded thought.
Eulogy for the Great Being in the Cliff Shrine

A slab of grey rock, sealed by moss and guarded by cloud: the Great Being’s Dharma-body is revealed within it, plain to the eye, with no concealment at all. Yet people seek him elsewhere — why is that?

A slab of rock, a lone peak, a clear pool, a white moon: the Dharma-body of freedom is originally without arising or ceasing. Form does not form itself; it is originally like an illusion — an empty flower before a filmed eye, lightning in a clear sky. It is not that the Great Being intends to do anything; it is the deluded who calculate in false thought. If you would see the Great Being’s true, original face, simply do not deliberate — the whole body appears of itself.
Eulogy for the Great Being Avalokiteśvara in Rock and Tree

Look at that grey cliff, towering and unmoved: it is truly my Great Being’s Dharma-body, standing alone and far. Look at the trees on the cliff, their branches and leaves spread thick: it is my Great Being’s shade of compassion, opening wide. He sits at ease within them, without speech or seeking, showing the thirty-two responses, wondrously answering everywhere. The sleeping multitude starts awake, yet he does not leave great samādhi; he pulls out every suffering and makes all pure. I contemplate the Great Being as thoroughly free of marks: in an illusory body he is named the most honored among the honored. He puts forth his broad and long tongue — mountains high, waters deep; day and night he ever teaches, and is named the Perceiver of the World’s Sounds.
Eulogy for the Responsive Transformations of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara

The Great Being’s body is like a maṇi jewel: the five colors appear in turn, and all is understood according to conditions. In heaven as a god, among humans as a human — since he is called the answerer of requests, why should he not show his form? If a son is sought, he answers as a man, adorned with merit, virtue, and wisdom beyond compare. It appears only in the seeker’s single mind; therefore it is named the inconceivable transformation.
Eulogy for Avalokiteśvara of Freedom

I bow to the Lord of Great Compassion, whose body of freedom is complete: a mirror image, the moon in water, doing deeds past thought. In the subtle dust of the Dharma-realm, one mote holds all lands, and every land as many beings as dust — nowhere does he fail to show his form. When a living being’s single thought is at leisure, he answers all at once and equally. As the chapter on perfect penetration says, this is still a matter of measure and number; only my own mind knows it — the Great Being is wholly unaware.
Moon-shadow and bell-sound, wondrous voice and form: the ear sees, the mind hears — merit beyond measure.
Eulogy for the Imperial Carving of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara

Our Great Being’s Dharma-body answers everywhere: through the gate of the ear-faculty he wondrously attains perfect penetration. Beat a drum in the ten directions and the ten directions hear it at once. In the emptiness of the Dharma-realm he manifests forms like clouds; in heaven above and the world below, no kind is left unentered. Therefore whoever seeks is fulfilled according to his mind. It is our gracious Empress Mother, endowed from former lives with the vow of compassion — like the Great Being’s mind, she practices wide skillful means, and by this wondrous image universally bestows on living beings, causing their wishes to be answered like an echo to a sound.
Eulogy for the Great Being Avalokiteśvara of Putuo

I hear the Great Being pervades without thinking, answering in lands as numerous as dust, practicing wide skillful means. Living beings are the mind; the mind is living beings. Therefore whoever seeks has only to call, and the sound is answered. As the water rises the boat floats higher; the more the mud, the greater the Buddha. The sharper the suffering, the deeper the compassion, with no leisure to receive and respond to all. He sits upon the rock of Potalaka, dwelling in the sea of birth and death: though space itself should melt away, this mind does not change.

He sits upon the Potalaka rock, contemplating the ocean of quiescence; everywhere he shakes the sound of the tide, and is named Avalokiteśvara Who Observes Freely. He puts forth his broad and long tongue, pervading the ten directions. Therefore whoever seeks appears at once as the thought arises. Living beings are already complete — why labor to go and save them? The water clears, the moon appears: neither before nor after.

Eulogy for the Great Being Avalokiteśvara in Celestial Robes

I bow to the Lord of Great Compassion, the perfectly complete and full Honored One, who sits at ease in the emptiness of the Dharma-realm, bright as the moon among stars, answering universally the minds of living beings, like the moon come over many waters. In the daily life of living beings his power is unknown; wishing to manifest a wondrous body, he borrows the painter’s hand. Painter and Great Being together enter the inconceivable: the shadow appears at the tip of a hair, like spring within a hundred flowers. In the most subtle and wondrous, the whole body appears at once, adorned with utmost beauty: necklaces of a hundred treasures’ light, celestial robes covering his form like thin mist shrouding the moon, as if within the white hair-mark. Seeing this rare mark, I bow and take refuge, and at once enter the ocean of quiescence. Know then that the seeker’s mind, pure as still water, stirs this wondrous body, and all is accomplished as the thought arises. By the vow from which this was born, may we together realize the vajra body, forever abiding to illumine the world, and be freed from every bond.
Eulogy for the Great Being Avalokiteśvara in Straw Robes

The Great Being is without marks — why then does he show himself so plainly? Straw robe and rush mat, complete just as he pleases. Beard and hair unkempt and scratched — not that he cannot cut them, but deliberately he leaves them, to pierce the eyes of the worldly. The Great Being is not worldly; the worldliness lies in the beholder. Like a flower in the air, it is the fault of the filmed eye. If one can remove the view of self, the Great Being is myself. Since he answers according to kind, what could be amiss? Again, like a place that hurts, only the one in pain knows it. If you would know the Great Being, neither the real nor the conventional will do.
